title: Scoggins v. Commissioner
court: United States Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit
subject: Realistic Prospect of Entering Business Under Section 174
summary: Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995), is a key Ninth Circuit I.R.C. § 174 ruling for founder-led R&D partnerships that contract research to a related corporation. Reversing the Tax Court, the court held that a partnership with a realistic prospect—objective intent and capability—of exploiting the technology in its own business could deduct its research expenditures.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Factual Matrix and Entity Architecture

In Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995), reversing T.C. Memo. 1991-263, 61 T.C.M. (CCH) 2859 (1991), the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit adjudicated a foundational dispute concerning the deductibility of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures incurred by a newly formed research partnership contracting with a sister corporate entity. The taxpayers, William V. Scoggins and Robert W. Christensen (joined on appeal by their spouses, Joyce M. Scoggins and Carrie L. Christensen, solely by virtue of filing joint federal income tax returns), had been actively engaged since 1972 in the business of designing, manufacturing, and operating epitaxial reactors. Within the semiconductor manufacturing industry, epitaxial reactors serve as specialized high-technology chambers used to deposit precisely controlled crystalline silicon layers onto substrate silicon wafers. Prior to the tax years at issue, Scoggins and Christensen had invented an epitaxial reactor, built a successful commercial enterprise around the technology, and marketed that product for about one and one-half years before selling the business for approximately $3 million, after which, pursuant to a covenant not to compete in the sales transaction, both inventors refrained from undertaking any significant developments in reactor technology for three years.

Following the expiration of that three-year period, Scoggins and Christensen structured a dual-entity arrangement in mid-1984 to develop a next-generation "pancake-heated" epitaxial reactor. Approximately two months before forming the partnership (that is, in or about June 1984), the two inventors incorporated Epitaxy Systems, Inc. (the corporation) to operate as a contract research and development provider, with Scoggins and Christensen holding a combined 75 percent controlling equity interest in the corporation. About two months later, in August 1984, Scoggins and Christensen formed the B & B Research and Development Partnership (the partnership), serving as its sole general partners. Scoggins and Christensen contributed to the partnership all the technology associated with the design and production of the new pancake-heated epitaxial reactor they had invented, together with personal capital, and the partnership agreement stated the partnership's purpose as engaging in the business, research, and development of semiconductor equipment (and in any other business the general partners deemed appropriate).

In August 1984, the partnership executed a written research and development agreement with the corporation under which the corporation agreed to perform the technical R&E work necessary to develop the new reactor. Under the financial terms of the contract, the partnership committed to provide up to $500,000 in research funding, structured as an initial upfront payment of $43,000 upon execution, followed by incremental progress payments advanced at the discretion of the partnership. Under the intellectual property provisions of the contract, the partnership retained absolute legal ownership of all resulting technology and inventions. Concurrently, the partnership granted the corporation two conditional commercial rights: first, a 15-month non-exclusive permissive license to market and sell the reactor technology worldwide in exchange for paying the partnership a 20 percent royalty on net sales; and second, an option to purchase all rights to the technology for a flat price of $5 million. The $5 million purchase option could not be exercised until 18 months after the technology reached final development—creating a three-month gap following the expiration of the 15-month non-exclusive license during which the corporation held no marketing rights—and remained open for a one-year exercise window. Exercising the $5 million buyout option required the corporation to pay at least $1 million in cash down, with the remaining balance (up to $4 million) payable via a promissory note secured by the research project and bearing interest at 110 percent of the applicable imputed interest rate periodically established pursuant to the Internal Revenue Code. Crucially, the partnership retained the indefeasible right to market the reactor technology directly (or license it to third parties) throughout the initial 18-month post-development window without bearing the 20 percent royalty cost imposed on the corporation, and retained the indefinite right to market the product if the corporation failed to exercise the $5 million option within its one-year window, although any licenses the partnership granted to others were subject to the corporation's option.
The Taxpayers' Claim and the Commissioner's Challenge

During the 1985 and 1986 taxable years, the corporation performed the contracted research under the daily technical supervision of Scoggins and Christensen, assisted by three corporate employees. On its federal partnership returns (Form 1065), B & B Research and Development Partnership claimed current R&E deductions under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 174(a)(1) of $290,000 for 1985 and $196,000 for 1986, totaling $486,000. Pursuant to standard partnership pass-through taxation principles under Subchapter K of the Code, the partnership itself paid no federal income tax; instead, Scoggins and Christensen reported their pro-rata distributive shares of the partnership's net losses resulting from the § 174 deductions on their respective individual joint income tax returns.

Upon examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue did not dispute that the $486,000 in expenditures were incurred for research and experimentation or that the enterprise was motivated by a genuine profit motive. Notwithstanding those concessions, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disallowed the § 174 deductions in their entirety. The Commissioner determined that the partnership could not have incurred the research expenditures "in connection with [its] trade or business" as mandated by I.R.C. § 174(a)(1), meaning its own trade or business (it was the Tax Court that subsequently characterized the partnership as only the investment vehicle for technology developed by the corporation, which would likely be exploited, if at all, by the corporation). Based on this disallowance, the Commissioner determined income tax deficiencies for 1985 and 1986 and added penalties for negligence and for substantial understatement of tax liability (the latter under former I.R.C. § 6661); the Scogginses' combined deficiency for both years totaled $175,448, and the Christensens' combined deficiency totaled $176,705.

body.text: Governing Statutory Framework and Final Holding

The statutory controversy centered on I.R.C. § 174(a)(1), which permitted a taxpayer to treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year "in connection with his trade or business" as currently deductible expenses not chargeable to a capital account. In federal R&D tax jurisprudence, the phrase "in connection with his trade or business" under § 174 is purposefully broader than the phrase "carrying on any trade or business" found in I.R.C. § 162(a) (governing ordinary and necessary business expenses) and I.R.C. § 41(b)(1) (governing the incremental credit for increasing research activities). In Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), the United States Supreme Court established that Congress enacted § 174 to equalize tax treatment between established corporations and startup enterprises by allowing immediate R&E deductions to up-and-coming businesses whose sole activity during the tax year is the research itself, prior to producing or selling any commercial goods. However, following Snow, the federal circuit courts—including the Ninth Circuit in Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993)—clarified that § 174 does not extend to passive investors financing the business of another entity. To satisfy § 174, a pre-revenue research entity must establish a "realistic prospect" of subsequently entering its own trade or business to exploit the fruits of the research if the project succeeds. Under Kantor, a taxpayer establishes a realistic prospect by demonstrating both an objective intent to enter such a trade or business and the capability of doing so.

At the trial level, the United States Tax Court (T.C. Memo. 1991-263) ruled in favor of the Commissioner, sustaining the disallowance of the $486,000 in § 174 deductions and affirming the § 6661 substantial understatement penalties while abating the negligence penalties. The Tax Court concluded that the partnership lacked a realistic prospect of exploiting the pancake-heated epitaxial reactor in a business of its own, pointing to the licensing and buyout option granted to the corporation, the partnership's lack of office equipment, telephones, and employees, and the absence of third-party licensing efforts during 1984 and 1985.

On February 1, 1995, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the Tax Court's decision. Writing for the appellate panel, Circuit Judge Hug noted that while the Tax Court's underlying factual findings are reviewed under the deferential "clearly erroneous" standard (Allen v. Commissioner, 925 F.2d 348, 353 (9th Cir. 1991)), the ultimate legal conclusion as to whether expenditures were incurred "in connection with a trade or business" under § 174 constitutes an application of law to fact subject to de novo appellate review (Zink v. United States, 929 F.2d 1015, 1020–21 (5th Cir. 1991)). Reviewing the contractual architecture and operational reality de novo, the Ninth Circuit held that the partnership possessed both the objective intent and the technical and financial capability to commercialize the reactor technology in its own trade or business. Consequently, the Ninth Circuit held that the § 174 deductions were properly taken and reversed the Tax Court's decision, which had upheld the deficiencies and the § 6661 additions to tax.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

Although the taxpayers in Scoggins ultimately prevailed on de novo appeal before the Ninth Circuit, the structural and evidentiary vulnerabilities in their transaction triggered a full IRS examination disallowance, an adverse trial verdict in the U.S. Tax Court, $352,153 in combined deficiencies (in addition to the negligence and substantial understatement penalties the Commissioner added), and several years of costly federal tax litigation (the appeal alone was argued in April 1993, deferred, resubmitted in January 1995, and decided on February 1, 1995). Furthermore, subsequent IRS administrative rulings—most notably Field Service Advice (FSA) 200145011 and Legal Advice Issued by Field Attorneys (LAFA) 20055203F—demonstrate how the Commissioner continues to deploy the analytical framework of Scoggins and Kantor to disqualify taxpayers whose R&D structures exhibit similar evidentiary or contractual weaknesses without the saving grace of Scoggins's and Christensen's personal technical dominance and high option pricing. Dissecting the specific legal, contractual, and documentation deficiencies alleged by the IRS and adopted by the Tax Court reveals the critical fault lines in federal R&D tax controversy.
Bifurcated Entity Architecture and the "Passive Investment Vehicle" Disqualification

The primary structural flaw that precipitated the dispute in Scoggins was the bifurcation of intellectual property funding from research execution across two separate legal entities formed within sixty days of one another. By forming Epitaxy Systems, Inc. in or about June 1984 to house the laboratory personnel and perform contract R&E, and subsequently forming B & B Research and Development Partnership in August 1984 to hold the technology and advance the $500,000 R&D budget, the taxpayers created a structure that superficially resembled the profile of a syndicated R&D tax shelter, although, as the Ninth Circuit emphasized, the partnership was composed not of passive investors but of the two inventors themselves. Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, the IRS systematically challenged limited and general partnerships that raised capital from high-income individuals, subcontracted 100 percent of the research to an operating corporation under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2) (which permits contract research incurred on behalf of the taxpayer), and passed immediate § 174 deductions through to the partners while shifting ultimate commercial manufacturing to the corporate contractor.

In sustaining the IRS's disallowance at the trial level, the Tax Court (which could not have relied on the Ninth Circuit's opinion in Kantor because, as the Ninth Circuit noted, that opinion had not been published at the time of the Tax Court decision) framed its inquiry as whether the partnership had realistic prospects of engaging in a trade or business, the standard applied to the disqualified arrangements in Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), Levin v. Commissioner, 832 F.2d 403 (7th Cir. 1987), Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988), and subsequently applied in Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993). In those precedents, courts established that while Snow eliminated the requirement that a taxpayer be currently producing or selling goods to claim a § 174 deduction, Snow did not eliminate the "trade or business" nexus altogether. Specifically, the prospective business must be the taxpayer's own business, not the business of the contract research corporation. When a partnership subcontracts all technical work to a controlled or third-party corporation and lacks a documented, autonomous operational roadmap showing how the partnership itself will transition from an R&D funding vehicle into a commercial manufacturer or active vendor, both the IRS and the Tax Court default to characterizing the partnership as a mere passive investor injecting risk capital into the corporation's business. In Scoggins, the Tax Court determined that the partnership was only the investment vehicle for technology developed by the corporation, which "would likely be exploited, if at all, by the corporation"; the Ninth Circuit rejected that conclusion on de novo review, finding that the partnership owned the technology, retained the right to market it, and had both the objective intent and the capability to enter the business.
Contractual Preclusion, Licensing Asymmetric Risk, and Purchase Option Economics

The second major deficiency identified by the Tax Court—and the focal point of all contract R&D litigation under § 174 and § 41—involved the terms of the August 1984 R&D and licensing agreement. The Tax Court concluded that by granting Epitaxy Systems, Inc. a 15-month non-exclusive worldwide license followed by an option, exercisable during a one-year window beginning 18 months after the technology was finally developed, to purchase all rights to the technology, the partnership had effectively contracted away its ability to exploit the epitaxial reactor in its own trade or business.

In federal R&D tax law, granting a research contractor an exclusive license or a bargain-priced buyout option is routinely fatal to the funding entity's tax claims. Courts evaluate whether the probability of the taxpayer entering into its own business rises above a "mere possibility" to a "realistic prospect" by scrutinizing the economic incentives embedded in the option mechanics at the time the contract is executed. In Kantor, for example, the research partnership spent $3.15 million developing computer software, yet granted the independent research contractor an option to acquire exclusive royalty-bearing rights to the software for a nominal payment of just $5,000. Because no rational commercial actor would decline to pay $5,000 to capture viable technology that cost $3.15 million to develop, exercise of the option was an economic certainty if the research succeeded, leaving the partnership with zero realistic prospect of ever commercializing the software itself.

In Scoggins, the Ninth Circuit concluded that the Tax Court erred in denying the deductions, and it contrasted B & B's contract with the nominal-option arrangement in Kantor, which had not been published when the Tax Court ruled. The Ninth Circuit rested its reversal in significant part on three interrelated contractual features that preserved the partnership's realistic prospect of independent commercialization. First, the buyout option erected a substantial economic hurdle: unlike the nominal $5,000 option in Kantor (representing 0.16 percent of the $3.15 million R&D budget), Epitaxy Systems, Inc. was required to pay $5 million (at least $1 million in cash, with the rest by a secured promissory note at 110 percent of the applicable imputed interest rate) to acquire technology funded by a $500,000 R&D budget—a 1,000 percent (10x) multiple of the research cost. The Ninth Circuit recognized that the $5 million price was not nominal in comparison to the research cost and was a significant impediment to the corporation's ability to engage in the business of marketing the technology; the research had to be successful enough for the corporation to amortize the purchase price and pay the royalty, and Scoggins and Christensen would have had to be willing to raise $5 million on the corporation's behalf, whereas the partnership could proceed without raising that capital or paying any royalty. Second, the partnership retained a royalty-free competitive advantage during the initial license window: because the 15-month license granted to the corporation was non-exclusive and burdened by a 20 percent net sales royalty payable to the partnership, the partnership retained the indefeasible right to market the reactor concurrently without paying that 20 percent royalty, placing the partnership in a superior cost position relative to the corporation during the initial 15 months. Third, the contract created an explicit exclusivity gap: between the expiration of the 15-month non-exclusive license and the opening of the purchase option window at month 18, there existed a three-month hiatus during which the partnership held 100 percent exclusive commercialization rights and the corporation held no marketing rights whatsoever.

However, practitioners must note how the IRS subsequently refined its audit posture regarding high option prices in FSA 200145011. When taxpayers in later transactions attempted to rely on Scoggins by inserting high dollar-value purchase options into R&D contracts while lacking independent operational capacity, the IRS explicitly ruled that determining whether a realistic prospect exists is not limited to "contractual preclusion" within the "four corners of the operative documents". In FSA 200145011, even though the contractor's option exercise price was substantial, the IRS disallowed the § 174 deductions because extrinsic evidence (including the Private Placement Memorandum) revealed that if the contractor declined the option, the taxpayer would exhaust its working capital by Year 5 and lacked the financial resources or infrastructure to complete development and market the product independently. Thus, under the IRS's approach, a high option price alone is insufficient; it must be paired with documented financial and operational capability to commercialize the technology if the option expires unexercised.
Absence of Physical Infrastructure, Facilities, and Direct Partnership Employees

A third evidentiary deficiency cited by the Tax Court in disallowing the deductions in Scoggins was the absence of office equipment, telephones, and employees inside the partnership. Specifically, during the 1985 and 1986 tax years, B & B Research and Development Partnership did not have office equipment or telephones and had no employees of its own that could engage in the business once the technology was developed (although Christensen owned his own equipment, which was available to the partnership should it need it). Meanwhile, the corporation had three employees who assisted in the research under the partners' guidance. From these facts, the Tax Court inferred that the partnership lacked the capability to engage in a business of its own, an element later articulated as the capability prong of the Kantor realistic prospect test.

While the Ninth Circuit rejected the Tax Court's reliance on these facts (observing that until the technology had been developed into a marketable product there was no need for office equipment or telephones, and that the partnership had the two key personnel, who were in a position to employ whatever marketing, manufacturing, or other personnel would be necessary), this factor remains a severe audit trap. The taxpayers in Scoggins survived the lack of partnership-level employees and office equipment because the two individual general partners (Scoggins and Christensen) were the inventors of the reactor, had been in the epitaxial reactor business since 1972, directed and guided the research on a daily basis, and had evidenced the financial ability to conduct the business (having previously developed, marketed, and sold their first reactor business for about $3 million, and having funded the research with their personal funds), placing them in a position to employ whatever personnel would be necessary once the technology was developed.

Where the funding entity's principals are passive financial backers, non-technical executives, or captive officers of the research contractor, the absence of partnership-level employees and facilities is fatal. For instance, in LDL Research & Development II, Ltd. v. Commissioner, 124 F.3d 1338 (10th Cir. 1997), and I-Tech R&D Limited Partnership v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-10, affirmed 335 F.3d 345 (4th Cir. 2003), the courts denied § 174 deductions where the partnerships lacked facilities and technical employees, holding that merely monitoring financial reports or attempting to secure royalty streams does not constitute active engagement or capability to enter a trade or business. Similarly, in FSA 200145011, the IRS disallowed § 174 deductions where the taxpayer had no facilities or employees and the operative agreements contractually prohibited the taxpayer from hiring experienced personnel away from the corporate contractor.
Pre-Commercialization Licensing Inaction and Contemporaneous Documentation Gaps

The fourth deficiency relied upon by the Tax Court was the partnership's failure to make any efforts during 1984 and 1985 to market or license the reactor technology to third parties. The Tax Court placed some emphasis on this commercial inaction as indicating that the partnership lacked realistic prospects of engaging in a trade or business of its own. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit overturned this inference, explaining that attempting to license or market an uncompleted, experimental semiconductor reactor prior to proving its technical feasibility would be premature, given the serious difficulties and competitive risks of marketing an epitaxial reactor that had not been fully developed.

Nevertheless, the Tax Court's focus on the lack of marketing or licensing activity highlights a documentation risk. The opinion does not indicate whether B & B Research and Development Partnership maintained formal contemporaneous commercialization plans, capital reserve budgets for post-prototype manufacturing, or partnership minutes documenting the specific commercial milestones at which the partnership would hire sales engineers or contract manufacturers (the Ninth Circuit noted only that the partners kept their own records and that the historical facts were not in dispute), but the Tax Court's reasoning illustrates how, absent such documentation, the IRS and a trial court may see little evidence of the funding entity's own commercial plans outside of the corporate contractor's activities. In modern R&D tax examinations, an absence of contemporaneous documentation demonstrating how the taxpayer plans to transition from experimental development to commercial exploitation routinely prompts the IRS to assert that the entity lacks an objective intent to enter a business.
Collateral Disqualification Traps Under I.R.C. § 41: "Carrying On" Nexus, Common Control, and Funded Research

From the perspective of a technical tax advisor, the dual-entity structure utilized in Scoggins—a partnership owned 100 percent by two founders contracting with a corporation owned 75 percent by those same founders—creates catastrophic collateral traps when claiming the incremental R&D tax credit under I.R.C. § 41. While Scoggins was litigated solely over R&E deductions under I.R.C. § 174(a)(1), contemporary taxpayers almost universally claim both § 174 treatment (mandatory capitalization and 5-year domestic or 15-year foreign amortization for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, or domestic expensing under amended rules) and the 20 percent incremental tax credit under I.R.C. § 41. Evaluating the Scoggins fact pattern under I.R.C. § 41 exposes three interrelated statutory hurdles regarding trade or business nexus, controlled group aggregation, and the funded research exclusion.

First, taxpayers must confront the stricter "carrying on" trade or business standard of I.R.C. § 41(b)(1). Unlike I.R.C. § 174, which requires only that expenditures be incurred "in connection with" a trade or business (satisfied by a realistic prospect of a future business under Snow and Scoggins), I.R.C. § 41(b)(1) restricts Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) to amounts paid or incurred in "carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer". Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(1) explicitly incorporates the strict I.R.C. § 162 standard for "carrying on," meaning the taxpayer must already be actively engaged in an existing trade or business at the time the QREs are incurred. Although Congress enacted a narrow exception in I.R.C. § 41(b)(4) treating the "carrying on" requirement as satisfied for certain startup taxpayers if the principal purpose in making the expenditures is to use the research results in the active conduct of a future trade or business, § 41(b)(4) applies exclusively to "in-house research expenses" (employee wages and supplies under § 41(b)(2)) and strictly excludes "contract research expenses" under § 41(b)(3). Because B & B Research and Development Partnership had zero employees and incurred 100 percent of its $486,000 R&D outlay as contract research payments to Epitaxy Systems, Inc., the partnership would be statutorily barred from claiming the § 41 R&D tax credit despite winning its § 174 deduction under Scoggins.

Second, the ownership proportions in Scoggins trigger a failure of the 80 percent common control aggregation rule under I.R.C. § 41(f)(1). Under I.R.C. § 41(f)(1)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6, all trades or businesses (whether or not incorporated) that are under "common control" are treated as a single taxpayer for purposes of computing the § 41 credit, allowing intercompany charges to be disregarded and the operating entity's active business and in-house wages to be aggregated with the IP holding entity. However, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6(a)(3)(ii) and I.R.C. § 52(b) (incorporating the brother-sister controlled group rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.52-1(d)), two entities are under common control only if the same five or fewer persons own a "controlling interest" (defined as at least 80 percent of the voting power or value of a corporation, and at least 80 percent of the profits or capital interest of a partnership) and an "effective control" interest (more than 50 percent identical ownership). In Scoggins, Scoggins and Christensen owned 100 percent of the partnership but only 75 percent of the corporation. Falling 5 percentage points short of the 80 percent controlling interest threshold prevents aggregation under § 41(f)(1), locking the two entities into separate-taxpayer status.

Third, because the 75 percent-owned corporation and 100 percent-owned partnership are treated as separate taxpayers under § 41, the structure runs headlong into the funded research exclusion and substantial rights trap under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). From the corporation's perspective (as the research performer receiving up to $500,000 from the partnership), under Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), the corporation cannot claim the § 41 credit unless it both bears the financial risk of failure (payment contingent on technical success) and retains "substantial rights" in the research results (meaning it need not pay for the right to use the research in its business). In Scoggins, the partnership retained sole ownership of the technology, and the corporation had to pay a 20 percent royalty or a $5 million buyout fee to use the technology. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), a contractor that must pay a royalty or purchase price to use the research results does not retain substantial rights. Consequently, under the Scoggins structure, the corporation is barred from claiming § 41 credits by the funded research and substantial rights exclusion, while the partnership is barred from claiming § 41 credits on the contract research because it is not yet "carrying on" an active trade or business under § 41(b)(1), creating a complete whipsaw forfeiture of the § 41 R&D tax credit.

cells: Trade or Business Nexus Under I.R.C. § 174(a)(1) ("in connection with his trade or business")

The partnership was a newly formed, pre-revenue entity that subcontracted 100% of R&E to a sister corporation; the Commissioner determined the expenditures were not incurred in connection with the partnership's own trade or business, and the Tax Court characterized the partnership as only the investment vehicle for technology developed by the corporation.

Reviewed de novo as a mixed question of law and fact (Zink). Under Snow and Kantor, a startup need not currently sell goods, but must prove a "realistic prospect" of entering its own trade or business using the R&E fruits, requiring both (1) objective intent and (2) capability.

Contemporaneous partnership/LLC operating agreements, commercialization roadmaps, and board minutes demonstrating a probability (not a mere possibility) that the funding entity itself will manufacture, market, or actively exploit the technology.
Contractual Preclusion & Licensing Rights (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2) Contract R&E)

The partnership granted the corporation a 15-month worldwide marketing license and a purchase option; the Tax Court held that the partnership had contractually precluded itself from exploiting the reactor.

The taxpayer must retain genuine legal and economic authority to commercialize the technology. In Scoggins, the 15-month license was non-exclusive and burdened the corporation with a 20% royalty, leaving the partnership free to market concurrently on a royalty-free basis, followed by a 3-month exclusive window.

R&D agreements must vest absolute IP title in the funding entity, avoid granting exclusive upfront commercialization licenses to the contractor, and preserve concurrent, unburdened marketing rights for the funding entity.
Technology Buyout Option Economics (Kantor Nominal Option vs. Scoggins Substantial Hurdle)

The Tax Court treated the corporation's option to purchase all technology rights (exercisable during a one-year window beginning at month 18) as part of the reason the technology would likely be exploited, if at all, by the corporation rather than the partnership.

Courts evaluate the economic probability of option exercise relative to R&D cost. Unlike Kantor ($5,000 nominal option after $3.15M R&D cost), the $5M buyout option in Scoggins (at least $1M cash down + a secured note at 110% of the applicable imputed interest rate, after $500k R&D cost; a 10x multiple) was a major financial hurdle that did not guarantee corporate exercise.

Any purchase option granted to a contractor must be priced at a substantial fair-market-value multiple of R&D spend with strict cash down-payment requirements, supported by an independent valuation showing exercise is not economically preordained.
Technical & Operational Capability (Absence of Employees, Telephones, and Office Equipment)
The Tax Court disqualified the partnership because it owned no office equipment or telephones and had zero employees of its own to manufacture or market the reactor post-development.

A research startup has no need for office equipment or telephones before a marketable product exists, and the partners were in a position to employ whatever marketing, manufacturing, or other personnel would be necessary. Capability was satisfied because the two general partners were the actual inventors (12+ years of reactor experience), directed daily R&E, and had evidenced the financial ability to conduct the business ($3M prior sale; personal funds financed the research).

Active, daily technical direction logs by the funding entity's principals; CVs proving domain mastery; absence of non-solicitation bars prohibiting the hiring of technical staff; and documented working capital reserves sufficient to fund post-R&D commercialization.
Pre-Commercialization Licensing & Marketing Efforts
The Tax Court cited the partnership's failure to solicit third-party licensees during 1984–1985 as evidence that it lacked realistic prospects of engaging in a trade or business of its own.
Not marketing or licensing technology to third parties before it has been fully developed is unremarkable, given the serious difficulties and competitive risks of marketing an undeveloped product.

Formal IP confidentiality protocols and staged commercialization schedules documenting why third-party marketing is deferred until technical uncertainty is resolved and prototype validation is complete.
Interplay with I.R.C. § 41 Credit: "Carrying On", Common Control (§ 41(f)(1)), and Funded Research (§ 41(d)(4)(H))

A 100%-owned partnership contracting with a 75%-owned corporation falls below the 80% common control threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6/§ 52(b), severing the entities for § 41 purposes and triggering the § 41(b)(1) "carrying on" bar and § 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion.

While § 174 requires only "in connection with" a prospective business (Snow/Scoggins), § 41(b)(1) requires actively "carrying on" a business, and the § 41(b)(4) startup exception covers only in-house QREs, not contract research; meanwhile, a contractor paying a 20% royalty or $5M buyout lacks "substantial rights" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2).

Align common ownership at ≥80% to qualify as a single taxpayer under I.R.C. § 41(f)(1)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6, or house W-2 researchers directly inside the IP entity to qualify as in-house QREs under § 41(b)(2) and § 41(b)(4).

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate the practical application of the legal principles established in Scoggins v. Commissioner—and to insulate taxpayers against both the Tax Court's evidentiary objections and the IRS's subsequent enforcement posture in FSA 200145011, LAFA 20055203F, and I.R.C. § 41 examinations—the following two industry case studies detail comprehensive, step-by-step remedial restructurings.
Case Study 1: Semiconductor Metrology Hardware Venture (Sister-Entity Contract R&D Between a Founder Partnership and a 75%-Owned C-Corporation)
Baseline Vulnerable Fact Pattern and Diagnostic Assessment

Two veteran optical physicists, Dr. Chen and Dr. Patel, previously designed wafer inspection systems for a major semiconductor equipment manufacturer and exited with $4 million in liquid capital. Following the expiration of their non-compete agreements, they seek to develop an autonomous Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) interferometric defect-detection chamber capable of identifying sub-2-nanometer crystalline slip defects on silicon carbide (SiC) wafers. Mirroring the exact architecture of Scoggins, Dr. Chen and Dr. Patel form two separate legal entities. The first entity is LithoMetrics R&D Partners LLC, taxed as a general partnership under Subchapter K and owned 50 percent by Dr. Chen and 50 percent by Dr. Patel (100 percent combined ownership), to which the founders contribute $1.2 million in cash and their preliminary optical schematics. The second entity is EUV Systems Corp., a Delaware C-corporation owned 37.5 percent by Dr. Chen, 37.5 percent by Dr. Patel (75 percent combined founder ownership), and 25 percent by an outside angel investor, which leases a cleanroom facility and employs five optical and mechanical engineers.

LithoMetrics R&D Partners LLC enters into a Research and Development Agreement with EUV Systems Corp., committing to advance up to $1.2 million on a time-and-materials basis for EUV Systems Corp. to build and test the prototype EUV metrology chamber. Under the draft contract, LithoMetrics LLC retains legal title to the intellectual property but grants EUV Systems Corp. an immediate 24-month exclusive worldwide license to manufacture and sell the completed system for a 10 percent royalty, plus an option exercisable at any time within 36 months to buy out 100 percent of the intellectual property for $150,000. LithoMetrics LLC has no employees, no physical office, no bank capital remaining after advancing the $1.2 million R&D budget, and no documented business plan for manufacturing. Both entities intend to claim I.R.C. § 174 deductions or amortization and I.R.C. § 41 R&D tax credits on the $1.2 million outlay.

Under Scoggins, Kantor, and I.R.C. § 41, this baseline structure will suffer catastrophic disallowance upon IRS examination across three distinct dimensions. First, the arrangement fails the Scoggins and Kantor option test: granting EUV Systems Corp. an exclusive 24-month license and a $150,000 buyout option against $1.2 million in R&D spending (a 12.5 percent nominal fraction, analogous to Kantor's $5,000 option on $3.15 million) guarantees that EUV Systems Corp. will exercise the option if the EUV chamber succeeds, stripping LithoMetrics LLC of any realistic prospect of entering its own business. Second, the arrangement triggers the capital exhaustion trap of FSA 200145011: because LithoMetrics LLC commits 100 percent of its $1.2 million capital to the R&D contract with zero reserve for post-development manufacturing or commercialization, the IRS will invoke FSA 200145011 to rule that the LLC lacks the financial capability to exploit the technology independently. Third, the structure falls victim to the I.R.C. § 41 whipsaw: because Dr. Chen and Dr. Patel own 100 percent of LithoMetrics LLC but only 75 percent of EUV Systems Corp., the entities fail the 80 percent controlling interest test under I.R.C. §§ 41(f)(1)(B) and 52(b) and cannot be aggregated as a single taxpayer under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6. As a standalone pre-revenue entity with only contract research expenses, LithoMetrics LLC fails the "carrying on" requirement of § 41(b)(1) and cannot use the § 41(b)(4) startup exception (which covers only in-house QREs). Simultaneously, EUV Systems Corp. cannot claim § 41 credits because its time-and-materials R&D is funded by LithoMetrics LLC and EUV Systems Corp. must pay a 10 percent royalty or $150,000 buyout to use the intellectual property, failing the "substantial rights" test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Project Governance and Entity Ownership Alignment

To eliminate both the Scoggins passive-vehicle characterization and the I.R.C. § 41(f)(1) separate-taxpayer whipsaw, the founders must execute comprehensive governance reforms prior to incurring R&E expenditures. First, the founders must align equity ownership to achieve at least 80 percent common control under I.R.C. § 41(f)(1)(B). They can accomplish this either by restructuring the angel investor's stake in EUV Systems Corp. so that Dr. Chen and Dr. Patel hold at least 80 percent of the voting power and value of EUV Systems Corp. (such as 40 percent each, with the angel investor holding 20 percent common stock or non-voting preferred convertible notes), or by admitting the angel investor as a 20 percent partner in LithoMetrics R&D Partners LLC so that the identical three persons own 100 percent (satisfying both the 80 percent controlling interest and greater than 50 percent identical ownership thresholds) of both entities under Treas. Reg. § 1.52-1(d). Once the 80 percent threshold is met, LithoMetrics LLC and EUV Systems Corp. are treated as a single taxpayer under I.R.C. § 41(f)(1)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6, allowing intercompany contract margins to be eliminated and the corporation's W-2 engineering wages and cleanroom supplies to qualify as in-house QREs eligible for the § 41(b)(4) startup rule. Concurrently, the LithoMetrics LLC Operating Agreement must be drafted to designate Dr. Chen and Dr. Patel as Managing Technical Partners with an explicit mandate to personally direct, supervise, and validate all EUV optical experiments on a daily basis, directly replicating the Ninth Circuit's decisive finding in Scoggins that the partnership consisted of "the two persons who were the most intimately involved in the development" of the reactor. Furthermore, transferring at least two key prototyping and commercialization engineers directly onto the W-2 payroll of LithoMetrics LLC ensures that the LLC possesses direct in-house human capital.
Step 2: Contractual Terms, Licensing Mechanics, and Buyout Option Restructuring

To satisfy the Ninth Circuit's Scoggins standard for I.R.C. § 174 deductibility or amortization on a standalone entity basis, the intercompany R&D Agreement must be rewritten to preserve the partnership's commercial primacy. The 24-month exclusive license must be replaced with a 15-month non-exclusive permissive license allowing EUV Systems Corp. to market the completed metrology chamber subject to a 20 percent royalty on net sales payable to LithoMetrics LLC. The contract must expressly stipulate that LithoMetrics LLC retains the indefeasible right to manufacture, market, and sell the EUV chamber directly to semiconductor foundries during and after that 15-month period on a royalty-free basis, giving LithoMetrics LLC a 20 percent pricing and margin advantage over the corporate contractor. Following the 15-month period, the agreement must establish a mandatory three-month exclusivity gap (months 16 through 18 post-completion) during which EUV Systems Corp.'s non-exclusive license expires and no purchase option is yet exercisable, vesting 100 percent exclusive commercialization authority in LithoMetrics LLC.

Furthermore, the nominal $150,000 option must be replaced with a one-year purchase option opening at month 18 priced at $12,000,000—mirroring the 10x ratio between the $5 million option price and the $500,000 research budget in Scoggins—supported by a contemporaneous third-party valuation memorandum projecting the net present value of a fully de-risked sub-2nm EUV inspection platform. Exercising that option must require at least $2,400,000 (20 percent) in immediate cash down upon exercise, with the remaining $9,600,000 evidenced by a senior secured promissory note bearing interest at 110 percent of the Applicable Federal Rate (AFR) under I.R.C. § 1274(d). Finally, to neutralize the IRS's personnel-lockout objection in FSA 200145011, the R&D Agreement must explicitly provide that if EUV Systems Corp. does not exercise the $12 million buyout option, LithoMetrics LLC holds the unrestricted contractual right to hire EUV Systems Corp.'s optical engineers and lease its cleanroom bays at fair market rates.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Commercialization Capability Substantiation

To preempt the Tax Court's critique regarding the lack of pre-development licensing efforts and physical office equipment, the founders must substantiate their commercialization capability contemporaneously. Rather than exhausting 100 percent of contributed capital on Phase 1 R&D, the founders should capitalize LithoMetrics LLC with $1.8 million, allocating $1.2 million to the discretionary R&D contract ceiling ($100,000 upfront plus milestone draws) and retaining $600,000 in an unencumbered partnership treasury account earmarked for initial commercial tooling, cleanroom assembly contracting, and technical sales hiring upon prototype completion, which directly defeats the capital-exhaustion argument of FSA 200145011. Simultaneously, the partners must adopt a formal Partnership Resolution at formation documenting a staged Go-To-Market (GTM) plan under which LithoMetrics LLC will directly market the EUV chamber to Tier-1 silicon carbide wafer fabs during the initial 18-month post-completion window, paired with a Trade Secret Protection Policy explaining that third-party licensing and customer demonstrations are intentionally deferred until the sub-2nm interferometric phase-shift algorithms are validated and provisional U.S. patent applications are filed with the USPTO, corroborating the Ninth Circuit's competitive-risk rationale.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Four-Part Test Compliance

To satisfy strict substantiation standards under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) and I.R.C. § 6001, the enterprise must maintain rigorous technical records. The partners must establish a project-level technical dossier for the "Sub-2nm EUV Interferometric Metrology Chamber" (the business component under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B)), documenting the baseline technological uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1): specifically, that existing optical inspection architectures cannot resolve sub-2nm subsurface slip planes in silicon carbide due to EUV thermal mirror distortion and stochastic photon shot noise. Dr. Chen and Dr. Patel must record contemporaneous weekly engineering directives, optical ray-tracing simulation logs, iterative mirror-coating test matrices, and failed prototype run sheets proving both a structured process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and the general partners' active, day-to-day technical control over the research under Scoggins. Finally, the venture must implement a project time-tracking and accounting system segregating direct engineering hours, consumable SiC test wafers (qualified supplies under § 41(b)(2)(C)), and discretionary progress advances under the $1.2 million R&D budget from general administrative, legal, and patent prosecution costs, which are excluded from § 174 and § 41 under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3).
Case Study 2: Biopharmaceutical Drug Discovery Syndicate (R&D Limited Partnership Contracting with an Established Biotech Sponsor)
Baseline Vulnerable Fact Pattern and Diagnostic Assessment

Vanguard Therapeutics, Inc., an established clinical-stage biotechnology C-corporation, seeks off-balance-sheet financing to develop a novel lipid-nanoparticle (LNP) mRNA delivery vector targeting hepatic stellate cells to reverse advanced liver fibrosis. Vanguard Therapeutics forms HepatoGen R&D Partners, L.P., a Delaware limited partnership in which a wholly owned subsidiary of Vanguard Therapeutics serves as the corporate General Partner (owning 1 percent of the partnership), while passive high-net-worth physician-investors contribute $8,000,000 as Limited Partners (owning 99 percent of the partnership).

Simultaneously at closing, HepatoGen L.P. executes three interlocking agreements with Vanguard Therapeutics. Under the Development Agreement, HepatoGen L.P. pays virtually all of its $8,000,000 capital ($7,850,000 after syndication fees) to Vanguard Therapeutics for Vanguard's scientists to conduct in-vitro assay screening and murine preclinical efficacy trials in Vanguard's laboratories, granting Vanguard sole authority to direct the research and file patent applications. Under a Non-Solicitation Covenant, HepatoGen L.P. is contractually prohibited from hiring any scientists or regulatory personnel employed by Vanguard Therapeutics. Under an Exclusive Option and Stock Purchase Agreement, Vanguard Therapeutics is granted an exclusive, irrevocable option to acquire 100 percent of the partnership's technology (or all partnership interests) upon completion of Phase 1 readiness in exchange for issuing $12,000,000 of Vanguard common stock or cash. According to the Private Placement Memorandum (PPM), if Vanguard declines the option, HepatoGen L.P. will have $0 remaining cash at Year 4 and will be forced to liquidate or find a third-party pharmaceutical company to fund Phase 2 clinical trials. HepatoGen L.P. claims $7,850,000 in I.R.C. § 174 deductions or amortization and passes the losses through to the physician limited partners.

This baseline structure represents the exact fact pattern where the IRS successfully distinguishes Scoggins and disallows 100 percent of the claimed § 174 deductions under FSA 200145011, Kantor v. Commissioner, Harris v. Commissioner, 16 F.3d 75 (5th Cir. 1994), and LDL Research & Development II, Ltd. v. Commissioner. First, the partnership suffers from a complete lack of independent control due to its captive general partner: unlike Scoggins, where the partnership's general partners were independent inventors controlling the contractor, here HepatoGen L.P.'s general partner is controlled by Vanguard's executives, meaning HepatoGen L.P. exercises zero independent governance over the research. Second, the partnership is incapable of commercializing the technology upon option non-exercise: even though the $12,000,000 option price appears substantial on paper, the IRS in FSA 200145011 explicitly ruled that a significant option exercise price cannot save a taxpayer when the PPM admits the partnership will run out of money ($0 reserve after paying the $7.85 million R&D fee), owns no wet-lab facilities, and is contractually barred from hiring the contractor's scientists. Because an early-stage LNP therapeutic vector requires tens of millions of dollars in subsequent FDA clinical trials before it can ever be sold commercially, HepatoGen L.P. has zero capability to enter a pharmaceutical manufacturing or commercial business of its own, reducing it to a passive financing conduit for Vanguard's pipeline.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Project Governance and Independent Technical Control Restructuring

To transform the syndicate from a passive financing conduit into an active joint development enterprise capable of surviving scrutiny under Scoggins and LAFA 20055203F, the partnership's governance must be severed from the corporate contractor. Vanguard's subsidiary must be removed as General Partner, and the entity must be structured as an operating LLC or partnership led by independent translational hepatology scientists and biopharmaceutical licensing executives who hold a meaningful equity stake and owe exclusive fiduciary duties to HepatoGen, eliminating the shared-officer conflict identified by the IRS in FSA 200145011. Furthermore, the operative agreements must strip Vanguard Therapeutics of unilateral control over the research protocol and patent prosecution by establishing a Joint Steering Committee (JSC) chaired by HepatoGen's independent Chief Scientific Officer (CSO). The JSC must set quarterly LNP formulation targets, approve murine dosing protocols, retain independent patent counsel to prosecute patents directly in HepatoGen's name, and hold the unilateral contractual right to reallocate research tasks to third-party Contract Research Organizations (CROs) if Vanguard misses technical milestones.
Step 2: Redefining the Target Trade or Business and Capital Adequacy

A critical technical nuance in biopharmaceutical R&D is defining a realistic commercial business model that matches the entity's capitalization. While a $10 million partnership cannot realistically build an FDA-inspected cGMP biologics manufacturing plant or single-handedly fund a $150 million Phase 3 clinical trial, it can realistically operate an active trade or business of developing preclinical LNP drug candidates across multiple fibrotic indications (hepatic, pulmonary, and renal fibrosis) and actively commercializing those delivery vectors through co-development joint ventures and active out-licensing with multiple pharmaceutical partners. Because Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), holds that merely collecting passive royalties on already-assigned inventions is not a trade or business, HepatoGen must actively conduct ongoing multi-indication R&E and retain active co-promotion and clinical supply rights. To eliminate the capital exhaustion defect of FSA 200145011, the partnership must cap the Vanguard R&D contract at $5,000,000—disbursed strictly in milestone tranches upon HepatoGen CSO sign-off, rather than an upfront $7.85 million lump sum, matching the discretionary funding structure of Scoggins—and retain $3,000,000 in an unencumbered partnership commercialization and clinical reserve to fund independent IND-enabling toxicology studies and direct business development if Vanguard declines its option, ensuring the Offering Memorandum demonstrates robust financial survival beyond Year 4.
Step 3: Contractual Terms, Option Scope, and Personnel Mobility

To prevent the buyout option from extinguishing the partnership's business, the scope and economics of Vanguard's option must be substantially narrowed. Rather than granting Vanguard an option to acquire 100 percent of HepatoGen's equity or all LNP platform intellectual property (which terminated the taxpayer's business in FSA 200145011), the agreement must restrict Vanguard's purchase option solely to the single field of Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH) liver fibrosis, leaving HepatoGen with 100 percent unencumbered ownership of the LNP delivery platform for pulmonary, renal, and oncology indications. Furthermore, the NASH indication buyout option must be priced at $35,000,000 (a 7x multiple of the $5 million R&D budget), payable with at least $10,000,000 in immediate cash (prohibiting stock-only exercise in thinly traded sponsor shares) during a 12-month window opening 18 months after IND clearance. During the initial 18 months following preclinical validation, Vanguard should receive only a non-exclusive license in hepatic fibrosis at a 15 percent net sales or sublicense royalty, while HepatoGen retains the concurrent right to commercialize the LNP platform across all other therapeutic fields royalty-free. Finally, the contractual prohibition against hiring Vanguard's scientists must be deleted and replaced with an affirmative right for HepatoGen to hire the lead formulation chemists if the option goes unexercised.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Substantiation Under I.R.C. §§ 174 and 41

Because HepatoGen is not under 80 percent common control with Vanguard Therapeutics, HepatoGen cannot aggregate with Vanguard under I.R.C. § 41(f)(1). Consequently, to claim the I.R.C. § 41 R&D tax credit prior to generating commercial revenue, HepatoGen must utilize the startup provision of I.R.C. § 41(b)(4), which applies exclusively to in-house research expenses under § 41(b)(2). HepatoGen must therefore directly employ its CSO and two formulation bioengineers on HepatoGen's own W-2 payroll, lease dedicated bench space in a biotech incubator facility, and purchase its own lipid reagent supplies directly, claiming the § 41 credit on those in-house QREs while amortizing or deducting the contract CRO payments under I.R.C. § 174. To substantiate the technical experimentation, the $5,000,000 Development Agreement must be structured into five discrete $1,000,000 technical milestones—such as achieving LNP encapsulation efficiency above 85 percent with a polydispersity index below 0.10, and achieving greater than 70 percent knockdown of COL1A1 mRNA in primary human hepatic stellate cells without hepatotoxicity—while documenting each hypothesis, lipid molar ratio permutation, dynamic light scattering (DLS) particle-size assay, and in-vivo histology readout in a centralized electronic laboratory notebook (ELN) contemporaneously signed by HepatoGen's CSO.

body.text: 5. Strategic Synthesis for U.S. Tax Practitioners

The Ninth Circuit's decision in Scoggins v. Commissioner stands as a pivotal bulwark for entrepreneurial technology ventures, confirming that inventors who bifurcate intellectual property ownership and contract research execution across closely held entities do not automatically forfeit their statutory right to treat R&E outlays as incurred "in connection with [a] trade or business" under I.R.C. § 174. However, the procedural history of the case—coupled with the IRS's aggressive post-Scoggins enforcement posture in FSA 200145011 and LAFA 20055203F—underscores that Scoggins is a narrow, fact-intensive precedent rather than a safe harbor or a blanket endorsement of contract R&D partnerships.

To prevail under the Scoggins and Kantor standard without enduring protracted Tax Court litigation, tax counsel must ensure that four foundational elements converge contemporaneously during the taxable years in which the research expenditures are incurred. First, the funding entity's principals must possess verifiable technical competence and exercise documented, day-to-day direction over the experimental process, distinguishing the entity from passive financial syndicates. Second, the operative R&D contract must vest outright intellectual property ownership in the funding entity and preserve an immediate, royalty-free right for the funding entity to market the resulting technology on superior or equal footing with any licensed contractor, reinforced by an exclusivity hiatus prior to any buyout window. Third, any purchase option granted to a research contractor must be priced at a substantial fair-market-value multiple of the R&D budget (such as the 10x multiple in Scoggins) with stringent cash down-payment requirements so that exercise is never economically preordained, while the funding entity maintains sufficient unencumbered working capital reserves and hiring mobility to commercialize the technology itself if the contractor declines the option. Finally, because satisfying the "in connection with" standard of § 174 under Scoggins does not automatically satisfy the stricter "carrying on" standard of § 41(b)(1) or the "funded research" exclusion of § 41(d)(4)(H), advisors structuring brother-sister R&D entities must align common ownership at or above the 80 percent controlling interest threshold of I.R.C. § 41(f)(1)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6, preventing intercompany contract arrangements from inadvertently disqualifying both entities from the federal R&D tax credit.

metaDescription: Scoggins v. Commissioner (9th Cir. 1995): a partnership with a realistic prospect of using the technology in its own business could deduct its research.
